description: Structured knowledge base created from the uploaded bond taxation report for support-assistant style answers.

rules.answer_scope: Answer only bond taxation, TDS, Form 168/Form 26AS, AIS, ITR mapping, tax reports, capital gains/losses, and related support-process questions based on this KB.
rules.tone: Professional, simple Indian English, customer-support ready, address as Sir/Madam when customer-facing.
rules.disclaimer: Wint Wealth is not a tax advisor. For personal tax filing treatment, the user may consult a CA or tax advisor.

chunks.section: Lifecycle of Bond Taxation
question_patterns: How are bonds taxed?
Explain bond taxation lifecycle
When does tax apply on bonds?
facts: Bond taxation can arise at multiple stages: receiving interest, selling before maturity, and maturity/redemption where purchase premium or discount affects capital gain or loss.
Interest is generally taxed under Income from Other Sources.
Selling before maturity may create capital gain or capital loss depending on sale value and acquisition cost.
At maturity, purchase premium or discount can create capital loss or capital gain when compared with face value/redemption value.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, bond taxation generally comes in three stages: interest payout, sale before maturity, and maturity/redemption. Interest is taxed under Income from Other Sources. If the bond is sold or redeemed at a value different from its acquisition cost, it may create capital gain or capital loss.

chunks.section: Interest Income Taxability
question_patterns: Is accrued interest taxable?
When is bond interest taxed?
Why platform accrued interest is not taxable?
How is coupon interest taxed?
facts: Interest is taxed when it is received from the issuing entity.
A platform may show accrued interest daily, but that daily accrued figure is not taxable merely because it is displayed.
Tax generally applies when the interest payout happens or when the bond is sold before maturity where accrued interest is part of the sale handling.
Example from KB: if accrued interest shown is ₹4,300 but interest received is ₹3,000, tax applies on ₹3,000 only.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, the accrued interest shown on the platform is only a running estimate. It is not taxable just because it is visible on the platform. Interest becomes taxable when the coupon/interest is actually paid by the issuer. For example, if the platform shows ₹4,300 accrued but only ₹3,000 is received as interest payout, the taxable interest is ₹3,000.

chunks.section: TDS on Bond Interest
question_patterns: Why was TDS deducted?
What is TDS on NCD interest?
When is TDS deducted on bond interest?
Why no TDS deducted?
facts: TDS is triggered when interest is paid.
The uploaded KB refers to Section 193 for Interest on Securities till 31 March 2026 and Section 393 from 1 April 2026.
TDS may not be deducted if interest is below the applicable threshold, typically ₹10,000 depending on issuer type and issuer process.
Even if TDS is not deducted due to threshold or issuer process, tax liability on interest income may still exist.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, TDS on bond interest is generally deducted when the issuer pays the interest. If TDS is not deducted, it may be because the issuer is following the applicable threshold rule, generally around ₹10,000 depending on issuer type and process. However, even if TDS is not deducted, the interest income may still need to be reported while filing ITR.

chunks.section: Gross Interest Reporting When TDS Is Deducted
question_patterns: Should user report gross or net interest?
Interest received after TDS what amount to show in ITR?
How to report interest when TDS deducted?
facts: If interest is ₹20,000 and TDS is ₹2,000, net received is ₹18,000.
While filing ITR, the user should report the gross interest amount of ₹20,000, not only the net amount received.
The TDS amount of ₹2,000 can be claimed as TDS credit while filing ITR, subject to Form 168/Form 26AS reflection and tax rules.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, the user should generally report the gross interest amount in ITR, not only the net amount received. For example, if interest is ₹20,000 and TDS is ₹2,000, the user receives ₹18,000, but the interest income to report is ₹20,000. The deducted ₹2,000 can be claimed as TDS credit while filing ITR, subject to it reflecting against the PAN.

chunks.section: Holding Period and Capital Gains Tax Rate
question_patterns: What is LTCG on bonds?
What is STCG on bonds?
What tax rate applies if held more than 12 months?
What if sold within 12 months?
facts: If a listed bond/NCD is held for less than or equal to 12 months, capital gain is treated as STCG and taxed at the investor's applicable slab rate.
If a listed bond/NCD is held for more than 12 months, capital gain is treated as LTCG and taxed at 12.5% as per the KB's Budget 2024 reference.
The KB states there is no minimum exemption threshold for LTCG on bonds; 12.5% applies to the full gain.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, the tax rate depends on the holding period. If the listed bond/NCD is held for 12 months or less, the gain is treated as short-term capital gain and taxed as per the investor’s slab rate. If it is held for more than 12 months, the gain is treated as long-term capital gain and taxed at 12.5%. The KB also notes that there is no minimum exemption threshold for LTCG on bonds.

chunks.section: Capital Gain or Loss Calculation on Sale
question_patterns: How is tax calculated if bond is sold before maturity?
What happens if I sell listed NCD?
How to calculate capital gain on bond sale?
Why capital gain on sold bond?
facts: For a sale before maturity, capital gain/loss is based on the difference between sale value and acquisition cost/investment amount.
If the sale amount is higher than purchase/acquisition cost, it is a capital gain.
If the sale amount is lower than purchase/acquisition cost, it is a capital loss.
Example from KB: Buy ₹50,000, sell ₹55,000, gain ₹5,000.
Interest received is taxed separately from capital gain. Example from KB: sell gain ₹4,000 and interest ₹1,000 are taxed separately.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, if a listed NCD is sold before maturity, the tax impact is based on capital gain or capital loss. The calculation is sale value minus acquisition cost. If the sale value is higher, it is a capital gain. If it is lower, it is a capital loss. The holding period then decides whether it is STCG or LTCG. Interest received is taxed separately under Income from Other Sources.

chunks.section: Capital Loss Set-Off and Carry Forward
question_patterns: Can bond capital loss be set off?
Can STCL be adjusted against LTCG?
Can LTCL be adjusted against STCG?
Can loss be carried forward?
facts: Short-term capital loss can be set off against both STCG and LTCG.
Long-term capital loss can be set off only against LTCG, not against STCG.
Capital loss can be carried forward for 8 years if declared in ITR.
Example from KB: STCG ₹5,000 and STCL ₹4,000 gives net taxable gain of ₹1,000.
Example from KB: if total loss is ₹10,000 and no gains exist in the same year, it can be carried forward for the next 8 years.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, capital loss from bonds can be adjusted only against capital gains as per the set-off rules. STCL can be set off against both STCG and LTCG. LTCL can be set off only against LTCG. If the loss cannot be fully used in the same year, it can be carried forward for 8 years, provided it is declared in the ITR.

chunks.section: Maturity Case - Face Value Returned
question_patterns: What is taxed at maturity?
Is principal repayment taxable?
What happens when bond matures?
facts: At maturity, the face value is returned.
If the bond is redeemed at face value and there is no premium/discount impact, only interest is taxed.
Principal repayment/return of capital is not taxed as interest income.
If acquisition cost differs from redemption/face value due to premium or discount, there may be capital loss or gain.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, at maturity, the face value/principal is returned. The principal repayment itself is generally a return of capital. Interest received is taxable. If the bond was purchased at a premium or discount compared with face value, the difference may also create capital loss or capital gain.

chunks.section: Bond Purchased at Premium
question_patterns: Why capital loss if bond matured?
What if bond purchased at premium?
Why tax report shows loss on maturity?
facts: If a bond is bought above face value, redemption at face value can create capital loss.
Example from KB: investment amount ₹1,01,000 and maturity face value ₹1,00,000 creates ₹1,000 capital loss.
Interest earned is taxed separately as interest income under Other Sources.
Capital loss can be adjusted only against capital gains as per ST/LT rules, and unused loss can be carried forward if eligible.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, if a bond was purchased at a premium, the acquisition cost is higher than face value. So when it matures at face value, the difference may appear as capital loss. For example, if the investment amount was ₹1,01,000 and maturity value is ₹1,00,000, the ₹1,000 difference is treated as capital loss. Interest earned is taxed separately as interest income.

chunks.section: Bond Purchased at Discount
question_patterns: What if bond purchased at discount?
Why capital gain on maturity?
How discount purchase is taxed?
facts: If a bond is bought below face value and redeemed at face value, the difference is treated as capital gain.
Example from KB: investment amount ₹90,000 and maturity at face value ₹1,00,000 gives ₹10,000 capital gain.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, if a bond is purchased at a discount, the acquisition cost is lower than face value. So when it matures at face value, the difference may be treated as capital gain. For example, if the investment amount was ₹90,000 and maturity value is ₹1,00,000, the ₹10,000 difference is treated as capital gain.

chunks.section: Deep Discount / Zero Coupon Bond Treatment
question_patterns: How is zero coupon bond taxed?
What is deep discount bond tax?
If zero coupon bond is sold before maturity?
facts: For deep discount/zero coupon bonds, the KB says if held till maturity, 10% TDS applies and income/repayment is considered Income from Other Sources taxed at slab rate.
The KB says if sold after holding for 1 year and before maturity, income is considered gain and LTCG applies at 12.5%.
The KB notes this applies to only one bond unit with limit up to ₹1 lakh.
This is a special-case rule and should be handled carefully.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, deep discount or zero-coupon bonds have a special tax treatment in the KB. If held till maturity, the KB treats the repayment/income as Income from Other Sources with 10% TDS and taxation at slab rate. If sold after holding for more than one year but before maturity, it may be treated as capital gain with LTCG at 12.5%. Since this is a special case, the user should validate personal filing treatment with a CA/tax advisor.

chunks.section: TDS Lifecycle and Form 168 Reflection
question_patterns: Why TDS not showing in Form 168?
When will TDS reflect?
What is TDS lifecycle?
Is TDS missing?
facts: TDS lifecycle: issuer deducts TDS, pays net interest to user, deposits TDS to government, files quarterly TDS return, data is processed by Income Tax department, then it reflects in Form 168 (previously Form 26AS).
Reflection in Form 168/Form 26AS generally happens around 10-15 days after the filing due date is completed.
A delay in Form 168/Form 26AS does not necessarily mean TDS is missing.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, TDS reflection is not instant. The issuer first deducts TDS, pays the net interest, deposits the TDS with the government, files the quarterly TDS return, and then the Income Tax department processes it. Only after this will it reflect in Form 168, previously Form 26AS. A delay in Form 168 does not always mean the TDS is missing.

chunks.section: Form 168 / Form 26AS Meaning
question_patterns: What does Form 168 show?
Does Form 26AS show total income?
Where is bond TDS visible?
facts: Form 168, previously Form 26AS, shows TDS deducted/tax credit details linked to PAN.
For bonds, relevant details can appear under TDS details such as Part A and section 193 entries.
Form 168/Form 26AS shows TDS deducted; it does not necessarily show total income fully.
Income must be declared separately while filing ITR.
If no TDS was deducted or issuer has not filed the return yet, it may not show.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, Form 168, previously Form 26AS, is mainly used to check TDS/tax credit details linked to the PAN. It shows TDS deducted and reported by the issuer, but it may not show total income completely. The user still needs to declare the income separately while filing ITR.

chunks.section: TDS Claim While Filing ITR
question_patterns: How to claim TDS?
Can user claim TDS in ITR?
How is deducted TDS adjusted?
facts: Users can claim/set off deducted TDS while filing ITR.
During ITR filing, the user reports total taxable income, tax liability is calculated, and TDS already deducted is set off from final payable tax.
TDS credit should be reconciled with Form 168/Form 26AS.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, the user can claim the TDS deducted while filing ITR. During filing, the user reports total taxable income, the tax liability is calculated, and the TDS already deducted is adjusted against the final payable tax. The user should reconcile the TDS credit with Form 168, previously Form 26AS.

chunks.section: Form 121 / Earlier Form 15G and 15H
question_patterns: What is Form 121?
Does Form 121 replace 15G and 15H?
Why TDS deducted after submitting Form 121?
facts: The KB says the government has proposed a new unified declaration form, Form 121, replacing Form 15G and Form 15H from FY 2026-27.
Earlier Form 15G was for non-senior citizens and Form 15H was for senior citizens.
The proposed Form 121 is age-neutral and intended to simplify declaration where total income is below taxable limit so TDS is not deducted on interest income.
Final acceptance and processing of the form is at the discretion of the NBFC/issuer.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, as per the KB, Form 121 is proposed as a unified declaration form from FY 2026-27, replacing Form 15G and Form 15H. The purpose remains the same: the user declares that total income is below the taxable limit so TDS should not be deducted on interest income. However, final acceptance and processing is at the discretion of the issuer/NBFC.

chunks.section: Reconciliation Framework - Bank Statement and Form 168
question_patterns: How to reconcile TDS?
What should user check for TDS mismatch?
How to compare platform report with bank and Form 168?
facts: Bank statement helps verify actual amount credited, interest payout received, net amount after TDS, whether repayment was received, actual credit date, and net payout amount.
Form 168/Form 26AS helps verify TDS deducted by issuer, TDS deposited with government, PAN-linked tax credit, whether TDS was officially reported, and amount eligible for tax credit while filing ITR.
Users should reconcile bond income and TDS across platform report, bank statement, Form 168/Form 26AS, and AIS where applicable.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, for reconciliation, the user should compare three things: the platform report, the demat-linked bank statement, and Form 168/Form 26AS. The bank statement confirms the actual net amount credited and credit date. Form 168 confirms whether the issuer has reported TDS against the user’s PAN. This helps identify whether the difference is due to timing, filing delay, or reporting mismatch.

chunks.section: Advance Tax / March 31 Accrued Entry Rule
question_patterns: Why April TDS not showing in current year Form 168?
Why May TDS is in previous FY?
TDS deducted in April but shown in previous year
What is March 31 rule?
facts: If TDS deducted in April/May does not match current FY Form 168/Form 26AS, it may be linked to income accrued at the end of the previous financial year, especially 31 March.
Some NBFCs file year-end interest or payments as advance tax/accrued entry.
The user should check the previous financial year's Form 168/Form 26AS and look for entries dated 31 March.
Tax credits are mapped to the period of earning, not only the payment date.
If April deduction relates to March earnings, it belongs to previous year's tax records.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, if an April or May TDS amount is not visible in the current financial year’s Form 168, it may be due to the March 31 accrual rule. Some NBFCs report accrued interest up to 31 March in the previous financial year. Please ask the user to check the previous financial year’s Form 168/Form 26AS and look for entries dated 31 March. If the April deduction relates to March earnings, it may be mapped to the previous year’s tax records.

chunks.section: Interest Payment Matching After Quarterly Returns
question_patterns: When will TDS details match?
Why platform report and AIS mismatch?
Why temporary difference in TDS?
facts: TDS details for interest payments generally match automatically once quarterly returns are processed.
If data does not appear immediately, allow the standard quarterly filing window.
Updates usually reflect by the end of the month following the quarter-end as per KB wording.
Timing differences can temporarily create differences between platform report, bank credit, AIS, and Form 168/Form 26AS until reporting is completed.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, the mismatch can be temporary because TDS details are updated only after the issuer files and the tax department processes the quarterly TDS return. Until that cycle is completed, there may be differences between the platform report, bank credit, AIS, and Form 168/Form 26AS. The details usually align once the quarterly reporting cycle is completed.

chunks.section: Quarterly Form 168 / Form 26AS Reflection Timeline
question_patterns: When will Q1 TDS reflect?
When will Q4 TDS show in Form 168?
What is quarterly TDS reflection timeline?
facts: Q1 April-June filing deadline is July 31, expected reflection around 15 August.
Q2 July-September filing deadline is October 31, expected reflection around 15 November.
Q3 October-December filing deadline is January 31, expected reflection around 15 February.
Q4 January-March filing deadline is May 31, expected reflection around 15 June.
TDS reflects only after the deductor files the quarterly TDS return and it is processed.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, Form 168/Form 26AS follows a quarterly TDS filing cycle. Q1 generally reflects around 15 August, Q2 around 15 November, Q3 around 15 February, and Q4 around 15 June, after the respective filing deadlines and processing. So TDS may not reflect immediately after the payout.

chunks.section: Conditions for TDS to Reflect Successfully
question_patterns: Why TDS is missing?
What conditions are needed for TDS to show?
PAN issue in TDS reflection
TRACES processing delay
facts: The deductor/entity must deposit tax with government within due dates, such as by the 7th of the following month in the KB example.
PAN must be correct; even one typo can cause the credit to go to suspense or another PAN/Form 168.
Filing alone is not enough; TRACES must process the return without default, usually taking 7-15 days post-filing.
Technical glitches and correction returns can also delay reflection.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, for TDS to reflect properly, three things should happen: the issuer should deposit the tax, the PAN should be correctly reported, and the TDS return should be processed by TRACES without default. If the PAN has even a small mismatch or if the return is still under processing/correction, the TDS may not reflect immediately.

chunks.section: Common Exceptions and Correction Returns
question_patterns: Why still not updated after filing?
How long correction return takes?
What are common TDS delays?
facts: Common exceptions include technical glitches.
The March 31 rule can cause TDS deducted in early April to relate to March income and appear in previous FY Form 168/Form 26AS.
If a correction return is filed, it can take an additional 1-3 weeks for the corrected amount to update in Form 168/Form 26AS.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, common reasons for delay include technical glitches, March 31 accrual mapping, or correction returns. If a correction return is filed by the issuer, it may take another 1 to 3 weeks for the corrected amount to reflect in Form 168/Form 26AS.

chunks.section: Checklist If TDS Is Missing
question_patterns: What to do if TDS is missing?
How to handle user asking Form 16A?
TDS not reflected escalation process
facts: First, check Form 168/Form 26AS.
Verify the correct Assessment Year; example in KB: AY 2026-27 for income earned between April 2025 and March 2026.
If TDS is not reflected in Form 168/Form 26AS, raise internally to TLs.
If user is adamant for Form 16A, raise it to the Asset team as per KB.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, please first check whether the user is viewing the correct Assessment Year in Form 168/Form 26AS. If the TDS still does not reflect after the expected quarterly timeline, this should be raised internally to TLs. If the user is specifically asking for Form 16A and is adamant, the request can be raised to the Asset team as per process.

chunks.section: Taxation Report Disclaimer
question_patterns: What disclaimer to add for taxation report?
Can user rely only on Wint tax report?
Is Wint tax statement tax advice?
facts: The tax statement is for reference and convenience only and is not tax advice.
Wint Wealth is not a professional/qualified tax advisor and does not guarantee accuracy of tax data.
Before filing ITR, user should reconcile the statement with Form 26AS/Form 168 and demat-linked bank account.
Tax treatment is based on standard treatment for listed and taxable bonds in India and may vary based on individual circumstances.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, the taxation report is provided for reference and convenience only. It is not tax advice. Before filing ITR, the user should reconcile it with Form 168/Form 26AS and the demat-linked bank account. Since actual tax liability may vary based on individual circumstances, the user may consult a CA or tax advisor before filing.

chunks.section: Master Report Purpose and Filing Mapping
question_patterns: What is Master Report?
How does Master Report help in tax filing?
Which report helps capital gains calculation?
facts: Master Report is a consolidated investment and taxation reference document.
It provides a complete view of bond holdings, repayments, transactions, and expected cash flows.
It helps with portfolio tracking, tax filing support, income reconciliation, capital gains calculation, and future cash flow planning.

Overall filing mapping: Repayment Summary = Interest Income + TDS, Sell Summary = Capital Gains/Loss, Holding Statement = reference only, Upcoming Cashflows = estimation only, Master Summary = portfolio and acquisition reference.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, the Master Report gives a consolidated view of bond investments, repayments, holdings, transactions, and expected cash flows. For tax filing, the Repayment Summary helps identify interest income and TDS, the Sell Summary helps calculate capital gains or losses, and the Holding Statement/Upcoming Cashflows are mainly for reference and estimation.

chunks.section: Master Report Fields
question_patterns: What fields are in Master Report?
Why acquisition cost is important?
How date of investment helps?
facts: Master Report fields include bond name, ISIN, number of units, invested amount, face value, acquisition cost, date of investment, maturity date, XIRR, frequency of interest payment, and frequency of principal repayment.
ISIN is used for verification and tax records.
Acquisition cost is used for capital gains calculation.
Date of investment determines holding period.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, the Master Report contains important details like Bond Name, ISIN, units, invested amount, face value, acquisition cost, date of investment, maturity date, XIRR, and repayment frequency. Acquisition cost helps calculate capital gain/loss, and date of investment helps decide the holding period.

chunks.section: Taxation Report Summary and Repayment Summary
question_patterns: What is shown in repayment summary?
How does taxation report help filing?
Why PAN matters in tax report?
facts: Taxation Report summary shows user identity details such as name, PAN, email, and demat account.
PAN linkage is critical because tax filing and TDS credit mapping happen through PAN.
Repayment Summary shows bond name, ISIN, interest paid, payment date, net amount received, and possibly TDS deducted.
Repayment Summary is used for Income from Other Sources in ITR.
If interest received is ₹18,000 and TDS is ₹2,000, user must report ₹20,000 gross interest.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, the Repayment Summary is mainly used to identify taxable interest income and TDS deducted. It shows details like bond name, ISIN, interest paid, payment date, net amount received, and TDS where applicable. While filing ITR, the user should report gross interest, not only the net amount received after TDS.

chunks.section: Maturity Details and Bonds Sold Tabs
question_patterns: What is Bonds Sold tab used for?
Where to report sold bond gain in ITR?
What is Maturity Details tab?
facts: Maturity Details shows bonds that matured during the year and includes bond name, ISIN, units, invested amount, principal repaid, maturity date, capital gains/loss, and holding period.
Bonds Sold tab represents realised capital gains or losses from selling bonds.
Bonds Sold information goes under the Capital Gains section in ITR.
User must determine STCG or LTCG based on holding period: less than 12 months = STCG/slab, more than 12 months = LTCG/12.5%.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, the Bonds Sold tab is used for realised capital gains or losses from selling bonds and this generally goes under the Capital Gains section in ITR. The Maturity Details tab helps cross-check bonds that matured during the year, including principal repaid, maturity date, capital gain/loss, and holding period.

chunks.section: TDS Summary Tab and Mismatch Explanation
question_patterns: What is TDS Summary used for?
Why TDS summary mismatch with Form 168?
Where to claim tax credit?
facts: TDS Summary shows name of issuer and total TDS deducted.
It represents tax already deducted on behalf of the user.
It is used for claiming tax credit in ITR.
This section should match Form 168/Form 26AS entries.
If there is a mismatch, possible reasons include issuer not filed yet or timing issue.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, the TDS Summary shows issuer-wise TDS deducted and is used for claiming tax credit in ITR. Ideally, it should match Form 168/Form 26AS. If it does not match, it may be because the issuer has not filed the quarterly return yet or due to timing differences in tax reporting.

chunks.section: Platform Report to ITR / AIS / Form 168 Mapping
question_patterns: Which report section maps to ITR?
Is principal repayment taxable?
Where does capital gain show in AIS?
How does platform report map to AIS?
facts: Repayment Summary maps to Income from Other Sources because it captures interest income.
Bonds Sold maps to Capital Gains because it captures profit/loss on sale.
TDS Summary maps to TDS Credit because it reflects tax already paid/deducted.
Maturity Details is used as a cross-check to ensure no missed income.
Principal repayment is not reported in Form 168/AIS as taxable income because it is return of capital.
Accrued interest at purchase is part of acquisition cost and not separately reported in AIS.
Accrued interest at sale may be taxed as interest in the year of sale if reported.
Upcoming future interest/principal is not earned yet and is not taxable yet.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, for filing, Repayment Summary is used for interest income under Income from Other Sources, Bonds Sold is used for capital gains or losses, and TDS Summary is used for claiming TDS credit. Principal repayment is generally return of capital and not taxable as income. Upcoming cashflows are only estimates and are not taxable until earned/paid.

chunks.section: FAQ - April Payout Not Visible in Current Year Form 168
question_patterns: My April payout is visible on platform but not Form 168
April TDS not in current year 26AS
Why April payout not visible in Form 168?
facts: April payouts fall under Q1 filing cycle, April-June.
Q1 filing due date is July 31.
Platform shows TDS immediately based on repayment date, but Form 168/Form 26AS reflects only after quarterly TDS return filing.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, April payouts fall under the Q1 filing cycle, which covers April to June. The issuer files the Q1 TDS return by July 31. The platform may show TDS immediately based on the repayment date, but Form 168/Form 26AS will reflect it only after the quarterly filing and processing is completed.

chunks.section: FAQ - No TDS Deducted Despite Interest Received
question_patterns: Why no TDS deducted even though interest received?
Interest received but no TDS
No TDS on bond interest
facts: TDS may not have been deducted because the issuing entity may be following the applicable ₹10,000 TDS threshold limit.
If total interest paid by that particular entity during the financial year does not cross the threshold, TDS may not be deducted.
Deduction process can vary depending on issuer internal compliance process and applicable regulations.
Tax liability on interest may still exist even if TDS is not deducted.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, TDS may not be deducted even though interest is received if the issuer is following the applicable ₹10,000 threshold rule. If the total interest paid by that particular entity during the financial year does not cross the threshold, TDS may not be deducted. However, the interest income may still need to be reported while filing ITR.

chunks.section: FAQ - Interest Reflected in Different Financial Year
question_patterns: Why interest reflected in different FY?
Interest accrued last year paid this year
Which year should interest be taxed?
facts: Interest income is generally taxed based on the actual repayment/payment date, not necessarily the period for which interest was earned/accrued.
If interest accrued over multiple months in one financial year but actual payment happened later, it may reflect in the next financial year.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, interest income is generally considered based on the actual repayment/payment date, not only the period for which it was accrued. So if interest was accrued over multiple months in one financial year but actually paid later, it may reflect in the next financial year.

chunks.section: FAQ - TDS Deducted After Form 121 Submission
question_patterns: Why TDS deducted after submitting Form 121?
Form 121 submitted but TDS still deducted
Can Wint stop TDS after Form 121?
facts: Final acceptance and processing of Form 121 is at the discretion of the NBFC.
Wint Wealth does not have access to the NBFC's internal systems.
Ability to intervene is limited if the form is not processed by the NBFC.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, even after Form 121 submission, TDS deduction depends on final acceptance and processing by the issuer/NBFC. Since Wint Wealth does not have access to the NBFC’s internal systems, our ability to intervene is limited if the form was not processed from their end.

chunks.section: FAQ - Capital Loss on Wint Tax Report
question_patterns: Why capital loss on tax report?
Why Wint shows capital loss?
Capital loss even though interest received
facts: A capital loss may appear if a bond was sold at a price lower than its investment amount.
A capital loss may also appear if the bond was purchased at premium and later redeemed/matured at face value.
Capital loss is separate from interest income.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, capital loss may appear in the Tax Report if the bond was sold below its investment/acquisition amount, or if the bond was purchased at a premium and later redeemed at face value. This capital loss is separate from interest income received on the bond.

chunks.section: FAQ - Accrued Interest Shown but Not Included in Taxable Income
question_patterns: Why accrued interest shown but not taxable?
Why accrued interest not in tax report?
Accrued interest visible on platform but not included
facts: Accrued interest displayed on the platform is not taxable merely because it is shown.
Interest is taxable when payout/repayment is received from the issuer.
If bond is sold before maturity, accrued interest handling may affect sale/tax reporting separately.
chunks.support_answer: Sir/Madam, accrued interest shown on the platform is a running estimate and is not taxable just because it is displayed. Interest is generally taxable when it is actually paid/credited by the issuer. That is why accrued interest may be visible on the platform but may not appear as taxable income until payout or applicable sale treatment happens.
